Scarce

/SKAIRS/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Scarce means insufficient for the demand — there isn't enough of it for everyone who needs or wants it.

Affordable apartments have become scarce in the city, with dozens of applicants for every listing.

Worked Example

During the microchip shortage, new gaming consoles became so scarce that stores sold out within minutes of each delivery.

Scarce captures the mismatch between supply and demand: plenty of people wanted consoles, but far too few existed to go around. That gap — not mere fewness — is what makes something scarce.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

insufficient: Insufficient means not enough to meet a specific need — insufficient funds for the withdrawal, insufficient evidence to convict. It measures one amount against one requirement. Scarce is social: there isn't enough for everyone who wants it, so people compete and go without. Scarce housing means many claimants, not one.

lacking: Lacking means absent or missing where it ought to be — a report lacking detail, a team lacking a goalkeeper. It points to a hole. Scarce says the thing exists but in amounts too small for the demand: water is scarce in a drought — present, precious, and fought over, not simply missing.

hard to come by: Hard to come by describes the hunter's experience: difficult to find or obtain, whatever the reason — good mechanics are hard to come by. Scarce names the cause on the supply side: too little exists for everyone who wants it. Things become hard to come by because they are scarce.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plentiful: existing in large amounts

abundant: more than enough for everyone

Where it sits · how badly the supply runs short — low → scarce → nonexistent

low vs. scarce: "Low" is milder than scarce — when supplies run low, there's still some left; when they're scarce, people are already going without.

nonexistent vs. scarce: "Nonexistent" is stronger than scarce — scarce water is desperately hard to find, but nonexistent water simply isn't there at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — scarce

Root — scarce: from Old North French 'scars,' likely from Vulgar Latin *excarpsus, 'plucked out' — the deeper origin is debated

Put it together

Put it together: Scarce came into English whole, through Old North French 'scars.' Its deeper Latin ancestry is genuinely uncertain, so there's no reliable prefix-root-suffix breakdown to memorize — the word is its own piece.

Use the root in a new word: scarcity

Use the root in a new word: scarcity: The scarcity of rain that summer turned the whole valley's fields brown.

Word Building

Word Choice

Neutral / descriptive

Scarce is about supply versus demand: something is scarce when there isn't enough of it for the people who want it (scarce housing, scarce fuel). Its neighbor in this unit, sparse, is about physical spacing instead — a sparse crowd is spread thin across the seats; scarce tickets are ones you can't get at all.
